JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA?

JPA is the specification (jakarta.persistence): annotations plus the EntityManager API. Hibernate is the most popular implementation and adds its own features (caching, @BatchSize, filters). Spring Data JPA is an abstraction on top of JPA that writes repository implementations for you (derived queries, paging, auditing).
What is the persistence context / EntityManager?

The persistence context is the set of managed entity instances, effectively a first-level cache keyed by id. The EntityManager is the API to it: persist, find, merge, remove, createQuery, flush. In Spring, a transaction-scoped context lasts for the duration of the transaction. Inside it, each id maps to one instance, and changes are written at flush through dirty checking.
ID generation strategies?

- IDENTITY: a DB auto-increment column (MySQL). Disables JDBC batch inserts.
- SEQUENCE: a DB sequence (Postgres, Oracle). The best for performance, because allocationSize lets Hibernate pre-allocate ids.
- TABLE: a separate table that simulates a sequence. Slow.
- AUTO: the provider picks.
- UUID: @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID) (JPA 3.1).
Explain relationships and owning side / mappedBy.

The types are @OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany. The owning side is the one that holds the foreign key (@JoinColumn). Only changes on the owning side are written to the DB. The inverse side declares mappedBy = "fieldName". In a bidirectional OneToMany/ManyToOne, the ManyToOne side is always the owner. ManyToMany uses @JoinTable. If the join table needs extra columns, model it as a separate entity.

What is the N+1 select problem? How to fix?

Loading N parents and then touching a lazy association on each one fires 1 + N queries. Fixes: JOIN FETCH in JPQL, @EntityGraph, Hibernate @BatchSize(size=50) or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size (uses IN queries), @Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT), or DTO projections. Detect it by turning on SQL logging or using Hibernate statistics.
Cascade types and orphanRemoval?

The cascade types PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH, ALL pass the operation from the parent to its children. orphanRemoval=true deletes a child once it's removed from the parent's collection. Use these only for real parent-owns-child (composition) relationships. Never put CascadeType.REMOVE on ManyToOne or ManyToMany.
JPQL vs Native Query vs Criteria API vs Derived queries?

- Derived: findByEmailAndActiveTrue. The query is generated from the method name.
- JPQL: queries entities and fields rather than tables, and is DB-independent.
- Native: @Query(value="…", nativeQuery=true) for DB-specific SQL.
- Criteria API / Specifications: type-safe dynamic queries (search filters). JpaSpecificationExecutor, or Querydsl.
CrudRepository vs PagingAndSortingRepository vs JpaRepository?

CrudRepository gives basic CRUD. PagingAndSortingRepository adds findAll(Pageable/Sort) (since Spring Data 3 it no longer extends CrudRepository). JpaRepository adds JPA-specific methods (flush, saveAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch, getReferenceById) and returns List instead of Iterable.
Does save() do insert or update?

SimpleJpaRepository.save() calls persist() if the entity is new (a null wrapper @Version; with no version field or a primitive one, a null id or a primitive id of 0) and merge() otherwise. With assigned (manual) ids, this means an extra SELECT before the merge. Implement Persistable<ID> to control what counts as new.
Optimistic vs Pessimistic locking?

Optimistic: a @Version column. The UPDATE includes WHERE version=?, and if another transaction changed the row you get OptimisticLockException and retry. Good when conflicts are rare. Pessimistic: @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) issues SELECT … FOR UPDATE, a DB lock. Good for heavy contention (inventory, wallets).
What causes LazyInitializationException? Fix?

Accessing a lazy association after the session or transaction has closed, for example in the controller or during JSON serialization. Fix: fetch what you need inside the transaction (JOIN FETCH or EntityGraph), map to DTOs inside the service, or use @Transactional on the service method. Avoid relying on Open-Session-In-View (spring.jpa.open-in-view=false is recommended) and don't use EAGER as a workaround.
Inheritance mapping strategies?

- SINGLE_TABLE (default): one table with a discriminator column. The fastest, but child columns must be nullable.
- JOINED: a table per class joined by PK. Normalized, but needs joins.
- TABLE_PER_CLASS: a full table per concrete class. Polymorphic queries need UNIONs.
- @MappedSuperclass: shares fields (id, audit columns) without being an entity.
What are projections? How to auditing (createdAt etc.)?

Projections fetch only the columns you need: interface-based (interface NameOnly { String getName(); }), class or record DTOs (select new com.x.Dto(o.id, o.total) …), or dynamic. Auditing: @EnableJpaAuditing plus @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy with @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class).
Why shouldn't you use Lombok @Data on entities?

Its generated equals/hashCode/toString include every field, including lazy associations. That triggers lazy loading, infinite recursion in bidirectional relationships, and broken behavior in Sets when the id changes after persist. Use @Getter @Setter instead, and write equals/hashCode based on the id or a business key.

orphanRemoval vs CascadeType.REMOVE?

REMOVE fires when the parent is removed. orphanRemoval does this too and additionally fires when a child is unlinked from the parent's collection. Use orphanRemoval only when the child cannot exist without this parent and is never moved between parents; moving a child to another parent may delete it, because it was removed from the old collection.
What is MultipleBagFetchException and how do you solve it?

A bag is a List mapped without an order column: an unordered collection that allows duplicates. Fetch-joining two bags in one query gives a Cartesian product of rows (10 items times 10 tags = 100 rows per order). Since bags allow duplicates, Hibernate cannot tell which rows are real and refuses at startup or query time.
- Best: run two queries in one transaction, each fetching one collection. The persistence context merges them into the same parents.
- Set hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size and fetch one collection or none.
- Change to Set: this stops the exception but keeps the Cartesian product, so it often only hides the performance problem.
What happens when you use pagination with a collection JOIN FETCH?

A LIMIT applied to joined rows would cut through a parent's children, so Hibernate cannot apply it in SQL. It loads all matching rows and paginates in memory, logging a warning (HHH90003004 in Hibernate 6, HHH000104 earlier). That can load a full table per request. Set hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch=true to turn it into an exception. Fix with the two-step pattern (page ids, then fetch by ids) or batch fetching. ToOne fetch joins do not multiply rows and are safe with paging.
Why is the inverse side of @OneToOne eagerly loaded even with fetch = LAZY?

For a null reference, Java needs null; for a present one, it needs a proxy. On the owning side the FK column tells Hibernate which applies. On the inverse side (mappedBy) there is no column in this table, so to decide between null and proxy Hibernate must query the other table anyway, and so it just loads the entity. Fixes: map only the owning side with @MapsId and look it up by the same id; bytecode enhancement; or, if the relationship is optional only in theory, optional = false, which helps in some mappings.
Why use Set rather than List for @ManyToMany?

When one element is removed from a List bag, Hibernate does not know which join row to target, because a bag has no identity per row. It deletes all rows for that owner and re-inserts the remaining ones. With a Set it removes exactly one row.

Why does a query trigger an UPDATE before it runs?

In AUTO flush mode, Hibernate flushes pending changes that could affect the query, so the query sees your own transaction's writes. This surprises people when validation queries inside a @Transactional method send half-finished entities to the database. If needed, a query can use setFlushMode(FlushModeType.COMMIT), but understand that it then may not see those changes.
What does @Transactional(readOnly = true) do with Hibernate?

Three things. Spring sets the Hibernate flush mode to MANUAL, so no accidental flush happens. Hibernate's session is set read-only, so entities loaded get no snapshot, which saves memory and dirty-check time. And connection.setReadOnly(true) gives the driver a hint, usable with routing to a read replica. It is not a security guarantee: a @Modifying query still runs unless the database rejects it. It also does nothing when joining an existing writable transaction.

Why not expose entities directly in REST responses?

- The API becomes coupled to the schema: renaming a column breaks clients.
- Lazy fields fail or trigger N+1 during serialization.
- Bidirectional links cause infinite recursion (@JsonIgnore and @JsonManagedReference are bandages).
- Internal fields leak (password hash, flags).
- Accepting entities as input allows mass assignment: a client can set role or version.
Map to request and response DTOs at the service boundary, by hand or with MapStruct.

Closed vs open interface projection, and why does it matter?

A closed projection exposes only getters that match entity properties, so Spring Data can select just those columns. An open projection uses @Value with SpEL, whose needs are unknown ahead of time, so the whole entity must be loaded and no query optimization is possible. Use a Java default method or a DTO instead when you want a computed field and fast queries.

@Modifying forgot clearAutomatically. What goes wrong? And why might it throw?

Without @Modifying at all, an update query throws, because Spring Data expects a SELECT. Without a transaction it throws TransactionRequiredException: custom repository methods are not covered by the default write transaction, so add @Transactional on the method or the calling service. Without clearAutomatically, managed entities keep old values, so a later findById in the same transaction returns stale data.
saveAll on 100,000 rows is slow. Why, and how do you fix it?

saveAll calls save in a loop. With IDENTITY, each row is one round trip and batching is disabled. With assigned ids, each row causes an extra SELECT through merge. All entities pile up in the context, so every flush checks more entities. Fixes:
- Use SEQUENCE with an allocation size matching the batch size, or JDBC directly for pure loads.
- Set hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50, hibernate.order_inserts=true, hibernate.order_updates=true.
- Process in chunks: flush() and clear() every 50, or one short transaction per chunk.
- Implement Persistable for assigned ids.
- For true bulk loads, use JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate or the database's COPY or LOAD command.
Explain the lock modes and when you would use OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT.

Scenario: Order has a cap on total value and items are separate rows. Two transactions each add an item. Neither changes the orders row, so its version does not change, and both commit, breaking the cap. Loading the order with OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT bumps the version even without a change, so the second transaction fails. This is how you make a whole aggregate behave as one consistency unit.

Two users edit the same record in a web form. How do you stop the second silently overwriting the first?

Send version to the client with the form (or as an ETag). On submit, the client returns it. The service loads the entity, compares versions, and on mismatch returns 409 Conflict or 412 Precondition Failed with If-Match. Merging a detached DTO-built entity containing the old version also triggers OptimisticLockException. Without a client-held version, each request reads a new version and the check protects only the few milliseconds between read and write.
What does a deadlock look like with JPA, and how do you avoid it?

Transaction 1 locks account A then wants B, while transaction 2 locks B then wants A. The database detects the cycle and aborts one (Spring raises CannotAcquireLockException or DeadlockLoserDataAccessException depending on database and version). Prevention: lock rows in a fixed order (sorted ids), keep transactions short, add indexes so locks cover fewer rows, and use lock timeouts. Hibernate's own flush order helps by ordering updates when hibernate.order_updates=true. Retry the whole transaction when it happens; the failed one left no effect.
How do you implement soft delete?

Hibernate 6.4+ has @SoftDelete, which turns removes into updates of a flag column and filters reads. Earlier, or for a deleted-at timestamp, combine @SQLDelete(sql = "update emp set deleted_at = now() where id = ?") with @SQLRestriction("deleted_at is null") (Hibernate 6.3+, replacing @Where, which is removed in 7). Consider: unique constraints must allow reinserts (a partial unique index), native queries do not get the filter, foreign keys still point to soft-deleted rows, and tables grow, so old rows may need archiving.
What are JPA lifecycle callbacks and entity listeners? When would you avoid them?

Callbacks are annotated methods run at state transitions: @PrePersist, @PostPersist, @PreUpdate, @PostUpdate, @PreRemove, @PostRemove, @PostLoad. They go on the entity or a class named in @EntityListeners. Typical use: set timestamps, normalize data. @PreUpdate runs at flush only if the entity is dirty. Pre callbacks must not call the EntityManager or change relationships; the spec leaves that behaviour undefined. They do not run for bulk statements. Keep business logic out of them, as it is invisible to readers.

A @Transactional method calls a slow REST API. The app stalls under load. Walk through the diagnosis.

Symptoms: hikaricp.connections.pending rises and requests time out with SQLTransientConnectionException: Connection is not available, even though the DB is idle. Each request holds a connection for the full HTTP call. With a pool of 10 and a 2-second partner call, throughput caps at 5 requests per second. Fix: read in one short transaction, call the API outside any transaction, write in a second short transaction, and use a version check to detect changes in between. Disable OSIV, or it extends connection use. Add a connection pool timeout and a client timeout. If the steps must be consistent, the outbox pattern moves the call out of the transaction entirely.
How can REQUIRES_NEW deadlock the connection pool?

The outer transaction holds connection 1 and the inner needs connection 2. If every pool connection is held by an outer transaction, all threads wait for a second connection that will never be released: a pool deadlock, ended only by the timeout. Make the pool larger than the max concurrency of nested calls, or remove the nested transaction. Also remember the inner transaction does not see the outer's uncommitted rows, and a lock held by the outer can block the inner forever within the same thread.
Does persisting a parent with a detached child work?

With CascadeType.PERSIST, no: the cascade reaches the detached child and Hibernate throws "detached entity passed to persist" (in Hibernate 7 this can appear as EntityExistsException). It happens when a DTO-built child carries an id. Without cascade, a reference to a detached entity works for a ManyToOne because only its id is needed; better, use getReferenceById. Calling save() when the parent has an id uses merge, which cascades MERGE instead.
@EntityGraph vs JOIN FETCH?

Both load an association in the same query. join fetch is part of the query text and can combine with conditions on the fetched data. Filtering on a fetched collection is risky, however: join fetch o.items i where i.qty > 1 gives you an entity with a partial collection, which looks complete, and could cause bad writes. @EntityGraph is declared separately, can be applied on derived queries and findAll, and always uses LEFT JOIN. Use the graph for reuse on simple queries, and fetch join for full control.
Does Spring Data's CrudRepository.findAll() on a mapped EAGER relation use one query?

No. findAll runs JPQL. EAGER mapping does not change JPQL's SQL, so eager ManyToOnes are then loaded with one extra query per distinct associated id. em.find by id, by contrast, uses a join for EAGER associations. That difference is why EAGER seems fine in a demo with findById and collapses on list pages.
How would you implement a search API with 8 optional filters?

Not with 256 repository methods, nor with (:name is null or e.name = :name) in one query, which can produce poor plans on some databases. Use Specifications, Querydsl or Criteria: build a list of predicates for only the filters provided. Add paging, a whitelist of sortable fields (a raw sort parameter can reference anything), a max page size, and indexes for the common filter combinations. Fetch to-one associations with an entity graph and project to a DTO. Query by Example (Example.of(probe)) is an alternative for equality-only filters.
Why does a @Transactional test hide bugs?

A test-level @Transactional keeps one persistence context open for the whole test and rolls back at the end. So lazy loading works where it would fail in production, the first-level cache answers reads so mappings are not really tested, flush may never happen, so constraints do not fire, and AFTER_COMMIT listeners never run. Call em.flush(); em.clear(); before assertions, or run without test transactions and clean up. Use Testcontainers with the real database rather than H2, since dialect differences hide real problems.
How does Spring Data decide the transaction for a derived query, and do two repo calls share a context?

Without a service-level transaction, each call opens its own transaction and context. Two findById(1L) calls then run two SELECTs and return two different instances (with OSIV on, the context is shared across the request, so they would be the same instance). Inside a service @Transactional, repository calls join it and share one context.
You see StaleObjectStateException in logs without any concurrent users. What might cause it?

Common causes beyond real concurrency: the same entity saved twice via different detached copies, a merge with an entity whose id was built by hand, the client re-sending an old version, a retry reusing a stale object, or a database trigger or bulk statement changing the version outside Hibernate. An update of a row that no longer exists gives the same failure, since zero rows matched. Log the id and both versions, and check for double submits.
How do you call a stored procedure with Spring Data JPA?

Use @Procedure on a repository method: @Procedure(procedureName = "apply_discount") void applyDiscount(Long orderId, BigDecimal pct);. Parameters map by position (or by name with @Param), and a single OUT parameter becomes the return value. For several OUT parameters or a result set, declare @NamedStoredProcedureQuery on the entity, or call em.createStoredProcedureQuery(...) in a custom fragment. Keep business logic in Java where possible; procedures are hard to test, version and port.
When would you use @ElementCollection, and what are its pitfalls?

For a collection of values with no identity of their own: tags, phone numbers, or embeddable addresses, stored in a child table via @CollectionTable. Pitfalls:
- A List without @OrderColumn is a bag: changing one element deletes all rows for the owner and re-inserts them.
- Elements cannot be queried, referenced or loaded on their own, and are always owned by the parent's lifecycle.
- Lazy by default, so the same N+1 and LazyInitializationException rules apply.
Prefer a Set (with proper equals/hashCode on the embeddable) or @OrderColumn; once the element needs its own id, audit columns or queries, promote it to an entity with @OneToMany.
save() of a duplicate email did not throw, but the transaction failed later. Why, and how should you handle unique-constraint violations?

save() usually only schedules the INSERT; the SQL runs at flush, typically at commit, after your try/catch has exited. The exception then surfaces as DataIntegrityViolationException from the transaction proxy. Options: call saveAndFlush() inside the try block when you need to react immediately; or let it propagate and map it to 409 Conflict in a @RestControllerAdvice. A pre-check with existsByEmail is good for a friendly message but is not enough on its own because of the race between check and insert; the unique index is the real guarantee. After the exception, the persistence context is unusable, so do not keep working in the same transaction.
You have two DataSources. Why does @Transactional on a method not roll back writes to the second one?

@Transactional uses one transaction manager, the @Primary one unless you name another with @Transactional("reportingTxManager"). Writes through the second EntityManagerFactory run in their own (or no) transaction, so they commit independently. Spring has no safe built-in way to make both atomic: ChainedTransactionManager is deprecated because a failure between the two commits still leaves them inconsistent. Use JTA/XA if you truly need it, or redesign with an outbox, idempotent consumers and compensation.
Spring Boot with virtual threads enabled: does JPA get faster?

Throughput for blocking I/O can improve because request threads are no longer scarce, but the connection pool becomes the limit: thousands of virtual threads will queue on a pool of 10 to 50 Hikari connections, and connectionTimeout errors appear instead of thread exhaustion. Keep transactions short, never hold a transaction across a remote call, and size the pool for what the database can handle, not for the number of threads. On JDKs before 24, synchronized blocks in older JDBC drivers or libraries could pin virtual threads to carriers; use current drivers and JDK 24+ where possible.
How do you route read-only queries to a read replica, and what is the catch?

Put an AbstractRoutingDataSource in front of the primary and replica pools, choose the key from TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly(), and wrap it in LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so the connection is picked after Spring has set the read-only flag. Then @Transactional(readOnly = true) services read from the replica. The catch is replication lag: a user who just saved something may not see it. Send reads that follow a write in the same flow to the primary, or route by a short "recent writer" window.
